idiom_name: session manager + CSPRNG identifier + server-side store + transport attributes + policy hooks
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one manager owns the life cycle - create (CSPRNG identifier, store record), validate (lookup, expiry, binding, principal), renew (new identifier, old one destroyed, data carried over), invalidate (delete the record). The transported value is an opaque identifier; state stays in the store. Set transport attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, host-bound name), drive idle and absolute expiry server-side, and call renewal from the authentication handler on every privilege change. Replace the single-process session table with the runtime's shared store abstraction as soon as more than one instance serves users.
code_sketch:
id = csprng(>=128 bits)                      # opaque, unpredictable
store.put(id, session{principal, created, expires, last_used})
s = store.get(request.token)                 # validate, never trust
if !s or expired(s) or !bound(s, request): reject
renew:  new_id = csprng(); store.move(old_id, new_id, s)
logout: store.delete(id); clear_cookie()
pitfalls: Identifiers generated with non-cryptographic randomness or reused across login make hijacking or fixation practical.
Client-side state that cannot be revoked: signed or encrypted cookies keep working after logout until they expire.
Expiry enforced on the client (cookie Max-Age alone) instead of in the store turns timeout policy into a suggestion.

Wrong move: leave a process-local session store (express-session MemoryStore, a per-instance in-memory map) in place behind a load balancer -> failure: a request lands on an instance that never saw the identifier, logged-in users are randomly treated as anonymous, and MemoryStore leaks memory and does not scale past a single process -> instead: move the store to a shared backing (Redis, JDBC, IDistributedCache) before adding a second instance.

Wrong move: treat a well-formed or signature-valid session cookie as proof of authentication and skip the per-request store lookup -> failure: logged-out, revoked or expired sessions keep working until the cookie's own expiry, breaking the fail-close guarantee the manager exists to provide -> instead: resolve every identifier against the store on each protected request and treat a miss or expiry as unauthenticated.

Wrong move: rotate only the current session identifier on a password change -> failure: sessions issued to the account on other devices keep the pre-change privilege state and stay usable until their timeout -> instead: invalidate all server-side sessions of that principal (or force reauthentication) on password or privilege change.
